DILG Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT DILG-NAPOLCOM Center, EDSA corner Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, QLæzon City http://www.dilg.com.ph DILG OPINION No. 23 s. 2021 10 February 2021 HON. JEREMY JONAHMAR G. PELAEZ Vice Governor, Misamis Oriental 2F Provincial Capitol Building, A. Velez St. Cagayan de Oro City Dear Vice Governor Pelaez: This has reference to your letter dated 14 February 2020 requesting for this Department's legal opinion regarding the recognition by the Sangguniang Panlalawigan of Misamis Oriental of Datu Salagaan Alan M. Mandokita as the Indigenous Peoples Mandatory Representative (IPMR). Per your letter, the recognition of Datu Salagaan Alan M. Mandokita as the Indigenious Peoples Mandatory Representative (IPMR) of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan of Misamis Oriental was tainted with irregularities, impropriety and malice, since there were questions of qualifications and existence of disqualifications. As a background, the DILG Provincial Office (PO) endorsed the "Certificate of Affirmation" of Datu Salagaan Alan M. Mandokita (Datu Mandokita) by the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) to the Sangguniang Panlalawigan, through the Office of the Vice Governor. The latter however, questioned the same by reason of violation of Section 1 1 (11 .I)(E), Article VII of the Higaonon Local Guidelinesl. By reason thereof, the Office of the Vice Governor conducted a Committee of the Whole Hearing wherein it was noted that there was no verified list of cities and municipalities which are qualified to allow mandatory 1 "The Provincial Legal Office called the attention of Mr. Mandokita's election as Barangay Chairman of Barangay Eureka, Gingoog City from August 16, 2002 to November 30, 2007 which qualifies him as politician which violates Section 1 1 (11.1 Article VII of the Higaonon Local Guidelines, disqualifying him as the Indigenous Peoples Mandatory Representative of the Province of Misamis Oriental."

representation of the IPs in the Sanggunian based on DILG-NCIP Joint Memorandum Circular No. 1, Series of 2011. Meanwhile, Datu Mandokita filed a Petition for Mandamus before the Regional Trial Court against the Sangguniang Panlalawigan of Misamis Oriental to compel the latter to recognize him as the IPMR and allow him to sit as Member of the Provincial Board, which was dismissed by the court on the ground that Datu Mandokita has already taken his seat as IPMR of Sangguniang Panlalawigan of Misamis Oriental. To begin with, this Department notes that the aforementioned Annexes in your letter were not attached. Nonetheless, we shall address the issues presented based on the documents forwarded to this Department. On the issue of mandatory representation of Indigenous Peoples (IPs) in sanggunian, Administrative Order (AO) No. 3, Series of 2018, entitled "Revised National Guidelines for the Mandatory Representation of Indigenous Peoples in Local Legislative Councils and Policy-Making Bodies", finds application. It is stated in Section 6 thereof, that the representation of ICs/lPs shall be in accordance with the following: "Where there exist an Ancestral Domain (AD) in a given LGU, IP representation is mandatory. The IPMR shall be selected, preferentially from qualified owners/rights holders of the AD. ICCs/IPs within the jurisdiction of the LGU who are not co-owners of an AD may participate in the selection or may be selected IPMR provided it is specifically allowed by the duly adopted Local Guidelines formulated by the owners of the AD. Where there are no AD, the rule on threshold applies. This is determined by the total population of an LGU divided by the number of Sanggunian members as prescribed in the Local Government Code, with the result/quotient to serve as the minimum to be met by an IP/ICC population in such LGU to qualify an IP mandatory representative for a seat in the Sanggunian. Where the situations in paragraphs a and b above are not obtaining, the concerned LGU may still allow representation in accordance with this Guidelines upon the initiatives of ICCs/IPs therein." (Emphasis supplied) In relation thereto, item 3.0 of DILG-NCIP Joint Circular No. 001, Series of 2011 provides for the guidelines with respect to the ICCs/lPs especially those who have identified and/or delineated their ancestral

domain/land areas and have determined that they are within the jurisdiction of local government units, to wit: "3.1 The total population of an LGU shall be divided by the number of sanggunian members as prescribed in the local government code and the result/quotient thereof will serve as the minimum number to be met by an IP/ICC population in such LGU to qualify an IP Mandatory Representative for a seat in the Sanggunian; 3.2 In the event that an IPP/ICC does meet the minimum number as computed under Item 3.1 of these Guidelines, the IP/CC land area shall be computed at five percent (5%) of the total land area of the LGU; 3.3 This minimum number computed under either Item 3.1 or 3.2 of these Guidelines shall be properly referred to as the "threshold". The NCIP, in coordination with the DILG, shall determine the local government units which have met the threshold; 3.4 If the threshold of IP/ICC population in a given LGU, as determined under Item 3.1 or Item 3.2 of these Guidelines are not met, this means that their will be no IP Sectoral representation in the sanggunian." In effect, AO No. 3, Series of 2018 amended DILG-NCIP Joint Circular No. 001, Series of 2011 to the extent that the rule on threshold shall only apply if there are no ancestral domain/s. Further, despite the existence or non-existence of ancestral domain, the LGU concerned may nonetheless allow representations of IP/ICC in accordance with AO No. 3, s. 2018. Hence, the contention that the recognition of Datu Mandokita as IPMR of the sanggunian was premature because of the "condition precedent' that the threshold must first be computed, is misplaced. Clearly, the rule on threshold cannot be regarded as a condition precedent for the selection of an IPMR. To reiterate, the rule on threshold shall be applied only if there is no ancestral domain to speak of. Even so, the LGU can still allow representations provided the same shall be in accordance with AO No. 3, s. 2018. With respect to the issue on qualifications and disqualifications, AO No. 3, s. 2018 likewise provides the general requirements for one to qualify as IPMR, as well as the grounds for an IPMR aspirant to be disqualified from selection, as provided in Section 8(A) and (B), and Section 9, respectively. Further, each community shall formulate its own guidelines for the selection of their IPMR in consonance with their customary laws, which must, at least, contain the qualifications, disqualifications, selection in policy making bodies, and removal process, among others.

Relative thereto, in case there is/are grounds for disqualification, a Petition for Disqualification may be filed in any appropriate offices of the concerned regionl, based on the following grounds: (a) those who are not qualified and who are disqualified under the local guidelines, (b) those who are not qualified and who are disqualified under this guidelines (National Guidelines), (c) commission of any of the prohibited acts under Section 21 , and (d) analogous circumstances2. On the other hand, a Protest may be filed in any appropriate offices of the concerned region, on the ground of (a) irregularity in the selection process and (b) validity of Certificate of Affirmation. Furthermore, Section 17(c) of AO No. 3, s. 2018 states that should a complaint arise by reason of the selection process, the Provincial Office (NCIP) or the Community Service Center, as the case may be, shall validate the facts and issues raised and submit a report and recommendation to the Regional Director (NCIP) within fifteen days from receipt of the complaint. Ergo, the issues regarding the process of selection of IPMR, qualifications of Datu Mandokita as IPMR of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan of Misamis Oriental, and the presence of disqualifications, must be filed before the Provincial Office of the NCIP or Community Service Center, as the case may be, for appropriate action in accordance with the process as provided for in Section 20(d) and (e) of AO No. 3, s. 2018. The foregoing position is however without prejudice to the position thereafter taken by the NCIP. We hope to have guided you accordingly. Thank you.
